How does the latency differ between RAG.snippet: # Long context vs RAG for real apps: costs, latency, and accuracy. We examine both long context language models (also referred to as long context models) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflows, which involve a two-step process of retrieving relevant information and generating responses. Long-context LLMs can handle context windows up to a million tokens, significantly larger than traditional models, enabling them to process extensive information in a single inference. There are two honest ways to give models more knowledge at inference time: make the context window bigger with long context models, or fetch the right text on demand using RAG workflows. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) retrieves relevant external documents to augment the model’s input dynamically, while long-context LLMs rely on a very large fixed context window to process all information directly. It refers to the maximum number of tokens the model can process in a single input prompt, including both user input and any additional context.

How does the latency differ between RAG.snippet: We believe that RAG is absolutely here to stay, but the architecture will evolve to accommodate long-context use-cases when needed. One big benefit from long-context is that developers won’t pull their hair out over what combination of chunking strategy, embedding model, and retrieval method they’ll need to use. When developers use RAG, it’s pretty easy to serve the model with up-to-date information from wherever they store company data. So to achieve best performance, developers should strategically place the most relevant documents at the start and end of the prompt, a task that can be very manual/complex if done with the long context approach. Beyond RAG and Long Context. RAG is here to stay and it will adapt to many new use-cases, and we might see a future where developers will be using a mix of long-context + RAG in their implementations. Our goal at Vellum is to enable developers to easily start, build and deploy production-ready AI apps, and our mission goes beyond just RAG or long context.

How does the latency differ between RAG.snippet: Long context approaches process every token through the model, while RAG selectively retrieves only relevant sections. For AI apps requiring interactive response times under 2 seconds, well-optimized RAG pipelines can often hit that target, while naive long-context prompting on very large inputs may struggle to do so. For retrieval-style queries where most context goes unused, RAG avoids paying for tokens the model doesn't need. Long context models tend to demonstrate superior performance for full-document understanding, while RAG often excels when factual accuracy, traceability, and cost constraints are primary concerns. Cost sensitivity matters most for retrieval-style queries, where RAG can operate at a fraction of long context costs. Route cost-sensitive queries through RAG while reserving long-context processing for tasks requiring full corpus analysis. Consider starting with RAG for cost-effective, fast retrieval over large knowledge bases—for retrieval-style queries, it can operate at a fraction of large context window costs.
